content_voiceover: This slide is a classic boards table on how to diagnose iron overload, and you need the numeric cutoffs cold. Serum ferritin is sensitive but non-specific, elevated above roughly two hundred to three hundred micrograms per liter in men and one fifty to two hundred in women, and it correlates reliably with total body iron only once it's above three thousand. Transferrin saturation of forty-five percent or higher actually precedes the ferritin rise, so it's useful for detecting early iron overload. For quantifying liver iron, MRI techniques including T2, R2 FerriScan, SQUID, and QSM estimate liver iron concentration, with iron overload defined above roughly three to seven milligrams of iron per gram dry weight, though the threshold is inconsistent across methods. Cardiac MRI T2 star below twenty milliseconds is the key predictor of cardiac iron overload and impending heart failure, so this is the test that tells you the heart is at risk, not the ferritin. And liver biopsy remains the gold standard, defined as greater than two milligrams of iron per gram dry weight, though it's invasive and largely reserved for research or discordant cases now. Don't forget the supporting workup: CBC with RBC indices, AST, ALT, and metabolic panels.
keypoints: Ferritin: sensitive, non-specific; correlates w/ iron store only >3000 mcg/L
TSAT ≥45% — rises before ferritin in early iron overload
Liver MRI (T2, R2, QSM): LIC >3-7 mg Fe/g dry weight
Cardiac MRI T2* <20 ms → best predictor of heart failure risk
Liver biopsy >2 mg Fe/g dry weight = gold standard
keypoint_voiceover: Key numbers to memorize: transferrin saturation forty-five percent or higher signals early iron overload before ferritin even rises. Cardiac MRI T2 star under twenty milliseconds is your best predictor of heart failure, so it drives management even when ferritin looks reassuring. Liver biopsy above two milligrams of iron per gram dry weight is still the gold standard, while liver MRI thresholds of three to seven milligrams are used non-invasively but are less standardized.
